definitions.definition: The giving of buying power, granted in exchange for a promise to pay it back.
The promise to pay back the credit; one person's asset and another's liability; a promise to pay a specific currency.

Whether fast credit/debt growth is good or bad hinges on what the credit produces and how the debt is serviced; borrowed money must be used productively enough to generate the income that services it. Too little credit growth can be as bad as too much (foregone opportunities).
Borrowing creates a cycle: spending more than you make now requires spending less than you make later; a logically driven series of events that recur in patterns.

Spending constrained only by lenders' and borrowers' willingness to extend/receive credit; availability controlled primarily by the central bank, which eases rates to end recessions. Produces mini-booms and recessions.

Short-term cycles add up to a long-term cycle because each cyclical high and low carries a higher debt-to-income ratio than the one before, until interest-rate cuts can no longer sustain the expansion (rate hits 0%) and deleveraging begins. More extreme than short-term cycles: higher debt burdens and less effective monetary policy.

Debt and debt-service costs rise faster than the incomes needed to service them, forcing a deleveraging; severe crises (depressions) occur when the central bank can no longer relieve them by lowering real and nominal rates.
A case in which real GDP fell by more than 3 percent; the 48 cases are all such cases in large countries over the last 100 years.

Policy makers cut rates; at about 0% that lever stops working; restructuring and austerity dominate without adequate stimulation (money printing, currency depreciation); debt burdens rise because incomes fall faster than debt is restructured, paydowns reduce the debt stock, and borrowers borrow to cover higher interest. Typical where the unsustainable debt was financed domestically in local currency: forced selling and defaults rather than a currency or balance-of-payments problem.

Occurs in countries reliant on foreign capital flows with significant foreign-currency debt that cannot be monetized; when inflows slow, credit creation turns to contraction, capital withdrawal dries up lending and liquidity while currency declines produce inflation. Especially hard to manage.
Debts rise faster than incomes and produce accelerating strong asset returns and growth, self-reinforcing because rising incomes, net worths and asset values raise borrowing capacity; unsustainable.
When prices have been driven by leveraged buying and the market is fully long, leveraged and overpriced, it is ripe for reversal; usually triggered by central bank tightening.

A reduction in debt/income ratios accompanied by acceptable inflation and growth: the four levers are balanced so that nominal growth rises above the nominal interest rate while activity and asset prices improve, without accelerating inflation, devaluing the currency or creating a new bubble.
Abusive use of printing/monetization and excessive devaluation (Weimar 1920s; Argentina and Brazil 1980s).
Late in the long-term debt cycle, when lower interest rates and central-bank purchases of debt assets no longer convert into spending; the phrase was coined in the 1930s.
Under accounting/regulatory rules the entity lacks enough equity capital to operate; it is 'broke'.

The entity lacks enough cash to meet its needs because its lenders are taking money away (a run); can occur with adequate capital if assets are illiquid. The trigger and main issue of most debt crises.
Largely unregulated non-bank lending institutions that develop during the bubble, outside the blanket of government protection.
Inflation so extreme that prices of goods and services at least double every year, accompanied by extreme wealth losses and severe economic hardship.
An increasing amount of money is being borrowed to make debt-service payments.
When the cost of debt service becomes greater than the amount that can be borrowed to finance spending, the upward cycle reverses.

Really bad debt losses: about 40% of a loan's value unrecoverable; such bad loans about 20% of all loans; so losses about 8% of total debt; total debt about 200% of GDP; shortfall about 16% of GDP. Socialized and spread over 15 years that is about 1% of GDP per year, which is tolerable; not spread out it is intolerable. So the downside of a large debt stock depends on policy makers' willingness and ability to spread the losses, which depends on (1) whether the debt is denominated in the currency they control and (2) whether they have influence over how creditors and debtors behave with each other.

It is possible for policy makers to manage debt crises well in almost every case where the debts are denominated in the country's own currency; the biggest risks are policy makers failing to do the right things (lack of knowledge/authority) and the political consequences of adjustments.

definitions.term: two long-term costs of a debt crisis
definitions.definition: (1) Losses from expected debt-service payments not being made (e.g., a 4% payment arriving at 2% or 0%, or a 50% loss if marked down); (2) the reduction of lending and the spending it financed going forward.

No single metric such as economy-wide debt/income or debt service/income can indicate an impending crisis; one must look at the debt-service abilities of individual entities and at concentration, especially in key entities.

deflationary_phases.name: 1) The Early Part of the Cycle
conditions: Debt growth strong but not faster than incomes because debt finances activities that produce fast income growth
Debt burdens low, balance sheets healthy; room for private sector, government and banks to lever up
Debt growth, economic growth and inflation neither too hot nor too cold: the 'Goldilocks' period

indicators.name: Nominal short rate
indicators.typical_reading: ~3.3% (chart)

policy: None specified; healthy levering up by all sectors
deflationary_phases.transition: Debts begin rising faster than incomes, starting the bubble
deflationary_phases.markets: Equities rising modestly; debt and debt service rising slowly
deflationary_phases.duration: About one year on the archetype axis (months -60 to -48); the up-wave as a whole runs for decades (p.17)

deflationary_phases.name: 2) The Bubble
conditions: Debts rise faster than incomes and produce accelerating asset returns and growth
Lenders size loans on projected income/cash flows, net worth/collateral and their own capacity to lend, all of which rise together
Over-extrapolation of a justified bull market; new buyers enter; confidence rises
Credit standards fall; banks lever up; shadow banking, new lending vehicles and financial engineering emerge; government guarantees encourage reckless lending
Asset-liability mismatches build: borrow short to lend long; liquid liabilities funding illiquid assets; risky assets bought with borrowed money; borrowing in one currency to lend in another
Debts rise fast and debt service costs rise even faster
Consensus is priced in and believed; crowd behavior and overweighting of recent experience produce extrapolation
Bubbles most likely at tops of the business cycle, balance-of-payments cycle and/or long-term debt cycle

indicators.name: Leveraging up
indicators.typical_reading: 20 to 25 percent of GDP over three years or so (p.18)

indicators.name: Total debt-to-income
indicators.typical_reading: averaged around 300 percent of GDP in the cases studied (p.19)

indicators.name: Debt growing faster than incomes (change during bubble)
indicators.typical_reading: 40% (range 14% to 79%) (p.19 table)

indicators.name: Debt growing rapidly (change during bubble)
indicators.typical_reading: 32% (range 17% to 45%) (p.19 table)

indicators.name: Income growth high but slower than debt (change during bubble)
indicators.typical_reading: 13% (range 8% to 20%) (p.19 table)

indicators.name: Equity markets extend rally (change during bubble)
indicators.typical_reading: 48% (range 22% to 68%) (p.19 table)

indicators.name: Yield curve flattens (SR - LR) (change during bubble)
indicators.typical_reading: 1.4% (range 0.9% to 1.7%) (p.19 table)

indicators.name: Nominal short rate
indicators.typical_reading: ~3.5% rising to ~4.5%; 'not much tightening until later in the bubble' (p.20 chart)

indicators.name: Interest payments
indicators.typical_reading: Increasingly covered by borrowing more rather than by income growth (p.20)

indicators.name: Equity price (indexed)
indicators.typical_reading: ~62 to ~100 (p.18 chart)

policy: Monetary policy typically helps inflate the bubble rather than constrain it, especially when inflation and growth are good (Japan late 1980s; world late 1920s and mid-2000s)
Central banks target inflation (or inflation and growth) rather than debt growth and fall behind the curve; Dalio argues they should target debt growth at a sustainable level
Well managed: central banks consider debt growth and asset markets, use macroprudential restraints where bubbles emerge, fiscal policy tightened (p.35)
Poorly managed: speculators and lenders over-extrapolate; central banks focus only on inflation/growth and keep credit cheap too long (p.35)
deflationary_phases.transition: Central bank tightening and rising rates (or an external liquidity tightening) begin to squeeze debt service; the top forms
deflationary_phases.markets: Equities rally strongly; debt/GDP rises rapidly; short rates drift up only late in the bubble; yield curve flattens
deflationary_phases.duration: Three years or so of leveraging up (p.18); months -48 to -12 on the archetype axis

deflationary_phases.name: 3) The Top
conditions: Market fully long, leveraged and overpriced; when things are so good they can't get better yet everyone believes they will, tops are made

Most often triggered by central bank tightening and rising rates; sometimes by the bubble itself (growth and inflation against capacity constraints), sometimes externally driven (reliance on external creditors; tightening in the currency the debts are denominated in; rise of the debt currency against the income currency); cash-flow shortfalls can also trigger
Debt-service squeeze hurts asset prices (negative wealth effect); new borrowing goes to debt service or isn't rolled; spending slows
Economy running at a high rate, demand pressing against capacity, unemployment at cyclical lows, inflation rising
Early on only parts of the credit system suffer, so weakening is not obvious while the central bank is still tightening

indicators.name: Credit/debt problems
indicators.typical_reading: Emerge about half a year ahead of the peak in the economy, in the most vulnerable and frothy pockets; riskiest debtors miss payments, credit spreads tick up (p.21)

indicators.name: Fastest rate of tightening
indicators.typical_reading: About five months prior to the top of the stock market (p.22)

indicators.name: Short rates
indicators.typical_reading: Peak just a few months before the top in the stock market; ~5% peak around month -6 (p.22, p.20 chart)

indicators.name: Yield curve
indicators.typical_reading: Rise in short rates narrows or eliminates the spread to long rates; flat or inverted; SR-LR ~+0.5% ('Tight') around month -8 (p.21-22)

indicators.name: Equity price (indexed)
indicators.typical_reading: Peak ~108 around month -6 (chart)

policy: Well managed: constrict the bubble with broad monetary policy or well-chosen macroprudential policies, then ease selectively (p.35)
Poorly managed: central banks continue to tighten well after bursting the bubble (p.35)
deflationary_phases.transition: Bubble pops; falling asset prices reduce equity and collateral of leveraged speculators, lenders pull back, runs from risky intermediaries; the depression begins when rate cuts hit the ~0% floor
deflationary_phases.markets: Equities peak and begin to fall; the more leverage and the higher the prices, the less tightening needed and the bigger the bust; post-bubble the wealth effect matters more than monetary policy and the early decline is mistaken for a buying opportunity

deflationary_phases.name: 4) The "Depression"
conditions: Interest rates cannot be cut materially because they are already close to 0% (or the floor is higher when currency outflows and currency weakness are great)
Debt defaults and restructurings hit leveraged lenders like an avalanche; runs on institutions without government protection; credit spreads rise so rate cuts don't help
Deflationary forces (defaults and austerity) dominate and are not balanced by money printing/monetization
Liquidity is the central concern; both solvency and cash-flow problems are present
Self-reinforcing loop: assets sold and spending cut to raise cash, asset values and collateral fall, incomes fall, creditworthiness falls faster than debts, lenders pull back
Debt burdens rise even as debts are written down because spending and incomes fall; household debt/net worth spikes
Not primarily psychological: driven by the supply and demand for credit, money, goods and services; credit appears in good times and disappears in bad times
Capitalists-investors lose real wealth and become defensive (move money out of the country, dodge taxes, seek government bonds, gold, cash); workers suffer collapsing incomes and job losses

indicators.name: Nominal short rate
indicators.typical_reading: Cut sharply toward 0%: ~5% to ~1.2% ('Easy') by about month 18, then ~1% (p.24 chart)

indicators.name: Yield curve (SR - LR)
indicators.typical_reading: ~-3% ('Easy') by months 24-36 (p.22 chart)

indicators.name: Equity decline
indicators.typical_reading: Typically around 50 percent (p.26); chart trough ~50 indexed near month 30

indicators.name: Bank leverage
indicators.typical_reading: About 12:1 or 15:1, so a 30% write-down is devastating (a 2:1-levered creditor loses 60% of net worth) (p.26)

indicators.name: Total debt (%GDP)
indicators.typical_reading: Keeps rising, ~265% to ~300% across the band (p.16 chart)

indicators.name: Household debt as % of net worth (US)
Bear-market rallies (Great Depression)
indicators.typical_reading: Six big rallies of 16 to 48 percent within a bear market that declined 89 percent in total, all triggered by government actions (p.28)

indicators.name: Gold price (local FX, indexed)
indicators.typical_reading: ~75 to ~150 across the band (p.34 chart)

indicators.name: Real FX vs trade partners
indicators.typical_reading: ~+1% to ~0% (p.33 chart)

policy: Four levers: austerity; debt defaults/restructurings; debt monetization/money printing; wealth transfers (haves to have-nots); key is to get the mix right
Austerity is tried first and fails: cutting spending cuts incomes; deficits widen anyway; governments raise taxes; both are big mistakes
Policy makers typically get the mix wrong initially (taxpayer anger, moral hazard), act slowly and in progressively larger doses; the longer they wait the uglier the deleveraging

When systemic failure looms, act immediately: curtail panic and guarantee liabilities (deposit/debt guarantees, injections, occasional deposit freezes); provide liquidity (lend against widening collateral to a wider set of institutions); support solvency of systemically important institutions (mergers, capital raising, accounting adjustments); recapitalize/nationalize/cover losses of systemically important institutions

Debt defaults/restructurings: swiftly recognize the magnitude; don't save every expendable institution; create or restore credit pipes; keep growth and inflation acceptable during the workout; decide whether to fix root causes or just restructure
Nonsystemic institutions absorb losses or fail: merged with healthy institutions in about 80% of cases, otherwise liquidated or transferred to an asset-management company

Creditor hierarchy: small depositors protected in nearly every case (depositors took losses in around 30% of cases, often on FX deposits converted at below-market rates); equity, subordinated debt and large depositors absorb losses; senior/sub-debt protection and dilutive recapitalizations mostly in the developed world; domestic private creditors sometimes prioritized over foreign, but IMF/BIS loans prioritized

Bad assets: transferred to an AMC in about 40% of cases, kept on the original lender's balance sheet in about 60%; disposal via restructuring, debt-for-equity swaps/seizures, direct sales, securitizations; AMCs publicly owned with targeted sale horizons (e.g., 10 years)

Systemically important borrowers kept intact via restructuring (debt-for-equity swaps, debt reduction, lower rates, terming out, new lending); nonsystemic borrowers restructure privately or go bankrupt; governments and AMCs relieve household debt

Regulatory reforms follow (deposit guarantees 1930s; Dodd-Frank and Volcker rule 2010; labor-market, credit-standard, competition, capital-requirement changes), for better or worse depending on politics

Redistribution: taxes on the rich become attractive; mostly income, property and consumption taxes; wealth/inheritance taxes raise little; transfers rarely contribute meaningfully without revolutions; the rich move money, hollowing out high-tax areas

Well managed: ample liquidity, rates to 0% quickly, aggressive monetization with targeted macroprudential policy, aggressive sustained fiscal stimulus easing past the turn, systemic institutions protected (p.35)
Poorly managed: slower cuts, limited liquidity, early tightening, delayed monetization, austerity, systemic institutions left damaged or failed (p.35)
deflationary_phases.transition: Shift to printing money, buying assets and providing guarantees in sufficient size moves the cycle from 'ugly deleveraging' to 'beautiful deleveraging'; typically two to three years into the depression
deflationary_phases.markets: Equities fall about 50% with intermittent policy-triggered bear-market rallies; credit spreads widen; runs on short-funded institutions; flight to government bonds, gold and cash; currency weakens
deflationary_phases.duration: Contraction averages 55 months (range 22 to 79) per the p.34 table; depression band months 0 to 36 on the archetype axis; US 2008 short-lived vs 1930s and Japan's lost decade prolonged

deflationary_phases.name: 5) The "Beautiful Deleveraging"
conditions: Four levers moved in a balanced way: enough printing/monetization and currency devaluation to offset austerity/defaults and lift nominal growth above the nominal interest rate, but not so much that inflation accelerates, the currency is devalued and a new debt bubble forms

Central bank provides liquidity and credit support, lends against a wider range of collateral (lower quality, longer maturity) and buys lower-quality/longer-term debt; government provides capital where needed
Income must grow faster than debt: with debt/income 100%, a 2% rate and 1% income growth the burden rises from 100/100 to 102/101
Printing is not inflationary when it merely offsets credit destruction; money creation replaces vanishing credit
All deleveragings studied eventually involved big waves of money creation, fiscal deficits and currency devaluations against gold, commodities and stocks
Pegged (gold/commodity/FX) systems run tighter policy until the pain forces them to break the link and print (Great Depression gold peg; easier in 2008)
In the end, policy makers always print: austerity causes more pain than benefit, big restructurings wipe out too much wealth too fast, transfers need revolutions

indicators.name: Money printing
indicators.typical_reading: Around 4 percent of GDP per year on average (p.34); Peak Money Creation (%GDP, ann) 4% (range 1% to 9%) (p.34 table)

indicators.name: Currency devaluation
indicators.typical_reading: Large initial devaluation of around 50 percent against gold (p.34); Size of FX decline vs. Gold -44% (range -58% to -37%) (p.34 table)

indicators.name: Fiscal deficit
indicators.typical_reading: Deficits widen to about 6 percent of GDP (p.34); Peak Fiscal Deficit -6% (range -14% to -1%) (p.34 table)

indicators.name: Timing of aggressive stimulation
indicators.typical_reading: Two to three years into the depression, after stocks have fallen more than 50%, economic activity has fallen about 10%, and unemployment has risen to around 10 to 15% (p.34)

indicators.name: Length of contraction
indicators.typical_reading: 55 months average (range 22 to 79) (p.34 table)

indicators.name: Money printing waves
indicators.typical_reading: Two classic waves: liquidity to stressed institutions, then large-scale asset purchases (p.33); money (%PGDP) rises to ~5% by month ~55 (p.33 chart)

indicators.name: Gold price (local FX, indexed)
indicators.typical_reading: Peaks ~195 around month 54 (p.34 chart)

indicators.name: Real FX vs trade partners
indicators.typical_reading: Falls to ~-4% by months 72-84 (p.33 chart)

indicators.name: Equity price (indexed)
indicators.typical_reading: Recovers ~55 to ~70 across the band (p.18 chart)

indicators.name: Change in debt-to-GDP ratio
indicators.typical_reading: Turns negative after about month 60 (p.19 chart)

policy: Right amounts of stimulus: (a) neutralize what would otherwise be a deflationary credit-market collapse, (b) get nominal growth marginally above the nominal interest rate so the deleveraging is spread tolerably
Avoid printing too much (ugly inflationary deleveraging: Weimar 1920s, Argentina and Brazil 1980s); harder when debt is in foreign currency and held by foreigners

Well managed: reflation begins with aggressive monetization through asset purchases or big currency declines; stimulative macroprudential policy protects systemic entities and stimulates high-quality credit; nonsystemic institutions allowed to fail in an orderly way; defaults/austerity balanced against monetization, currency declines and fiscal stimulus (p.35)

Poorly managed: monetizations stutter and start; purchases muted and cash-like with no wealth effect; central bank undermined by fiscal austerity; over-indebted nonsystemic entities protected (zombie banks, malaise); faith in the currency allowed to collapse with too much printing (p.35)
Those who printed quickly and well (US 2008-09) did much better than those who did it late (US 1930-33)
deflationary_phases.transition: As rate cuts and asset purchases lose effect the cycle enters 'pushing on a string'; recovery proceeds toward normalization
deflationary_phases.markets: Debt/income ratios decline while activity and financial asset prices improve; nominal growth exceeds nominal rates; gold and currency devaluation reflect the reflation
deflationary_phases.duration: Months 36 to ~78 on the archetype axis; stimulation begins two to three years into the depression

deflationary_phases.name: 6) "Pushing on a String"
conditions: Lowering interest rates and central-bank purchases of debt assets have diminished effect; low growth and low returns on assets
Both interest rates and risk premiums on risky assets are low, so MP1 and MP2 are at their limits ('little gas in the tank'); e.g., 1937-38 and the present (2018) in the US
Risk: too much printing/monetization and too severe devaluation relative to deflationary alternatives produces an ugly inflationary deleveraging
Prolonged monetization can lead people to question the currency as a store hold of value and move to alternatives such as gold; monetization swaps one IOU (debt) for another (printed money)

indicators.name: Monetary Policy 1 (MP1)
indicators.typical_reading: Interest-rate driven; most effective and broadest (wealth effect, cheaper credit purchases, lower debt service); stops working when short rates hit about 0%

indicators.name: Monetary Policy 2 (MP2)
indicators.typical_reading: Quantitative easing: printing money to buy financial assets, typically debt; works through investors/savers, not spenders; widens the wealth gap; most effective when risk and liquidity premiums are large and fades as they compress; if private credit growth doesn't pick up, policy is pushing on a string

indicators.name: Monetary Policy 3 (MP3)
indicators.typical_reading: Puts money more directly into spenders' hands with incentives to spend; continuum from coordinated fiscal-monetary action to helicopter money; most effective when fiscal and monetary policy are coordinated

policy: MP3 forms with precedents: (1) debt-financed fiscal spending, sometimes paired with QE buying most of the issuance (Japan 1930s; US WWII; US and UK 2000s)

(2) debt-financed fiscal spending where the Treasury isn't on the hook: central bank prints to cover debt payments (Germany 1930s) or lends to non-government entities for stimulus projects (development banks in China 2008)

(3) no debt issuance; newly printed money given directly to the government to spend: printing fiat currency (Imperial China, American Revolution, US Civil War, Germany 1930s, UK WWI) or debasing hard currency (Ancient Rome, Imperial China, 16th-century England)

(4) printing money and direct cash transfers to households ('helicopter money'; US veterans' bonuses in the Great Depression; Imperial China): equal or targeted amounts; one-off or ongoing (universal basic income); use-it-or-lose-it within a year; directed to retirement/education/small-business accounts; or distributing QE returns to households instead of to the government
(5) big debt write-down accompanied by big money creation (the 'year of Jubilee'): Ancient Rome, the Great Depression, Iceland

Most effective approaches involve fiscal/monetary coordination so both providing and spending of money occur; helicopter money alone is less adequate than money with incentives to spend; a tax break is probably not helicopter money depending on financing
Macroprudential policies (regulatory control of credit cost/availability for targeted parts of the system) are valuable in all seven stages; detailed in the Appendix
deflationary_phases.markets: Low returns on assets; risk premiums compressed; cash can look appealing versus overpriced assets; possible shift to gold if monetization is prolonged
deflationary_phases.duration: Not quantified; occurs in the later years of the long-term debt cycle

deflationary_phases.name: 7) Normalization
conditions: The system gets back to normal, though recovery in activity and capital formation is slow even after a beautiful deleveraging
Investors take a very long time to become comfortable holding equities again (equity risk premiums stay high)

indicators.typical_reading: Roughly 5 to 10 years (the 'lost decade') (p.38)

indicators.name: Stock prices regaining former highs
indicators.typical_reading: Around a decade (p.38)

indicators.name: Length of equity drawdown (months)
indicators.typical_reading: 119 average (range 60 to 249) (p.38 table)

indicators.name: Length of GDP drawdown (months)
indicators.typical_reading: 72 average (range 25 to 106) (p.38 table)

indicators.name: Change in debt-to-GDP post-stimulation
indicators.typical_reading: -54% average (range -70% to -29%) (p.38 table)

indicators.name: Total debt (%GDP) at month 84
indicators.typical_reading: ~270% vs ~305% peak (p.16 chart)

policy: Continued stimulation and reform; no specific new levers
deflationary_phases.markets: Equities ~80 indexed at month 84, still below the ~108 peak; debt-to-GDP ratio falling ~10% per year by month 84
deflationary_phases.duration: 5 to 10 years for activity; about a decade for equities

inflationary_phases.name: 1) The Early Part of the Cycle
conditions: Favorable capital flows from good fundamentals: competitiveness and productive investment opportunities; debt levels low, balance sheets healthy

Exports attract foreign capital that funds productive investment; debt and incomes rise at comparable rates; debt and equity markets strong; private sector, government and banks borrow sensibly as incomes rise fast

Currency cheap and balance of payments favorable: demand for the currency exceeds supply, so the central bank gets more growth per unit of inflation and can appreciate the currency, lower rates and/or accumulate reserves
Central banks often sell their currency for the inflows and build foreign-exchange reserves (savings that cushion currency swings); accumulating reserves is stimulative
Currency total return attractive to foreigners

indicators.name: Capital flows
indicators.typical_reading: The most important flows to watch because they are the most volatile (p.41); ~4-6% of GDP inflows (chart)

indicators.name: Current account (%GDP)
indicators.typical_reading: ~-3% (p.44 chart)

indicators.name: GDP gap
indicators.typical_reading: ~+1% (p.44 chart)

indicators.name: Real FX vs TWI
indicators.typical_reading: ~0% (p.45 chart)

policy: Central bank may intervene to sell its own currency and accumulate FX reserves to limit appreciation
inflationary_phases.transition: Strong fundamentals and early levering up set up a boom that attracts more capital; the bubble begins
inflationary_phases.markets: Currency appreciates and/or reserves rise; asset prices rise; influx of money stimulates the economy
inflationary_phases.duration: Months -60 to -48 on the archetype axis

inflationary_phases.name: 2) The Bubble
conditions: Self-reinforcing virtuous cycle of strong capital inflows, good asset returns and strong economic conditions; currency and/or asset prices bid up and increasingly debt-financed; debts rise rapidly relative to incomes

Exchange rate strong, FX reserves increasing, economy booming; total returns to foreigners (local asset returns plus currency appreciation) very attractive; the country becomes the hot place to invest; investors who were never involved rush in
Entities build structurally long currency positions (foreign subsidiaries hold unhedged local deposits; locals borrow in the weaker foreign currency because foreign bankers are eager to lend)

Fewer productive investments with more capital chasing them; rising currency erodes competitiveness; growth increasingly financed by debt rather than productivity; heavy reliance on foreign financing shows up as rising foreign-currency debt (undeveloped local financial system, distrust of local-currency lending, small domestic savings)
Income-spending gap widens; growth depends on ever-larger inflows; the country becomes fragile so even a minor event can trigger reversal

indicators.name: Foreign capital inflows
indicators.typical_reading: High, on average around 10 percent of GDP (p.42)

indicators.name: FX reserves
indicators.typical_reading: Central bank accumulating reserves (p.42); ~85 to ~112 indexed (p.48 chart)

indicators.name: Real FX
indicators.typical_reading: Bid up and overvalued on a PPP basis by around 15 percent (p.42); ~+17% vs TWI at the peak (p.45 chart)

indicators.name: Stocks
indicators.typical_reading: Rally on average by over 20 percent for several years into their peak (p.42); ~75 to ~120 indexed (p.52 chart)

indicators.name: Consumption and trade
indicators.typical_reading: Foreign capital finances a consumption boom; imports rise faster than exports; current account worsens (p.42)

indicators.name: Debt/GDP growth
indicators.typical_reading: Rises at an annual rate of about 10 percent over three years (p.43)

indicators.name: Foreign-currency debt
indicators.typical_reading: Rises to around 35 percent of total debt and around 45 percent of GDP (p.43)

indicators.name: GDP gap
indicators.typical_reading: Very strong, around +4 percent, growth well above potential, tight capacity (p.43)

indicators.name: Debt/GDP over the bubble
indicators.typical_reading: Rises from around 125 percent to about 150 percent (p.43)

indicators.name: Current account over the bubble
indicators.typical_reading: Deteriorates by about 2 percent of GDP (p.43); ~-6% of GDP at the top (chart)

indicators.name: Nominal short rate
indicators.typical_reading: Drifts down ~22% to ~15% (p.48 chart)

policy: Central bank accumulates reserves; monetary policy typically not tightened enough (as in the deflationary bubble)
inflationary_phases.transition: Inflows slow (naturally or via a shock) and the combination of high currency, high asset prices and high debt growth becomes unsustainable; the top forms
inflationary_phases.markets: Currency appreciates ~17% real; equities rally strongly; capital inflows peak ~11% of GDP; current account ~-6% of GDP; GDP gap ~+5%
inflationary_phases.duration: About three years of fast leveraging (p.43); months -48 to -12

inflationary_phases.name: 3) The Top and Currency Defense
inflationary_phases.months: -12 to 0 (defense phase about six months around the top)
conditions: The flows that caused the bubble, the high currency, high asset prices and high debt growth become unsustainable; a mirror-opposite spiral of weakening inflows, weakening asset prices and deteriorating conditions sets in: a balance of payments crisis and an inflationary depression
Because optimism is priced in, even a minor event can slow inflows and raise domestic outflows; adverse capital-flow shifts matter more than trade balances

Causes of the top-reversal: income from selling to foreigners drops (currency too strong, commodity price fall); costs of imports or borrowing rise; capital inflows decline (unsustainable pace slows, worries about economic/political conditions, monetary tightening in the local or debt currency, or tightening abroad); citizens/companies want to get their money out
Weakening capital flows are often the first shoe to drop; they cut the investment and consumption they financed, borrowers look less creditworthy, foreigners lend less (self-reinforcing)
Asset/currency holders fear capital restrictions and rush out; policy makers fear a currency collapse; the central bank's trade-off worsens (less growth per unit of inflation)

indicators.name: Growth
indicators.typical_reading: Slows relative to potential as capital inflows slow (p.46)

indicators.name: Domestic capital outflows
indicators.typical_reading: Pick up a bit (p.46); ~-3.5% of GDP at month 0 (p.51 chart)

indicators.name: Exports
indicators.typical_reading: Export earnings fall (prices or quantities); exports typically flat, no longer rising (p.46)

indicators.name: Capital inflows
indicators.typical_reading: Roll over from ~11% of GDP peak (p.46 chart)

indicators.name: Interest-parity arithmetic
indicators.typical_reading: An expected 5% annual depreciation needs 5% higher rates; a 5% expected monthly depreciation needs about 80% annualized (80 not 60 because of compounding); a 5-10%/yr expected depreciation implies an intolerable 5-10% rate premium (p.47)

indicators.name: Forward vs spot
indicators.typical_reading: Forward price declines ahead of spot as the rate differential widens (whip-like effect); after the currency is let go, spot catches up and the forward rallies relative to spot (p.48)

indicators.name: Duration of currency defense
indicators.typical_reading: Relatively brief, in the vicinity of six months (p.48)

indicators.name: Reserves drawn down during defense
indicators.typical_reading: About 10 to 20 percent before the defense is abandoned (p.48); ~112 to ~105 indexed by month 0 (chart)

indicators.name: Nominal short rate
indicators.typical_reading: Turns up from ~15% to ~20% at month 0 (p.48 chart)

policy: Central banks typically defend the currency by (a) spending down reserves to fill the balance-of-payments deficit and/or (b) raising interest rates; these defenses and managed currency declines typically don't work because they give sellers a better exit without moving the currency/rates to sustainable levels

A managed decline with falling reserves makes the market expect further depreciation, pushing up domestic rates (a tightening in a weak economy), encouraging withdrawals and devaluation speculation, widening the BoP gap and forcing more reserve sales or abandonment of the planned path
A reserve-based defense must stop because no sensible policy maker runs out of savings; policy makers (especially peg defenders) make boldly confident vows just before letting the currency go

Capital controls are a third, often last-ditch lever that seldom works: investors find ways around them and the attempt to trap capital makes people want to escape (bank-run analogy); at most a temporary fix
inflationary_phases.transition: The defense is abandoned and the currency is let go, usually after about six months and a 10-20% reserve drawdown
inflationary_phases.markets: Asset prices fall and interest rates rise; the forward currency leads the spot down; reserves decline; equities roll over from ~120 to ~110 indexed
inflationary_phases.duration: Months -12 to 0; currency defense about six months

inflationary_phases.name: 4) The Depression (Often When the Currency Is Let Go)
conditions: A country, unlike a family, can change the amount and value of its currency; a 30% devaluation is a 30% pay cut only relative to the rest of the world, so currency declines offer price cuts to the world without domestic deflation
After unsustainable support (reserves, tightening, strong assurances, sometimes FX controls), policy makers stop fighting and let the currency decline, generally trying to smooth its fall

After letting go, people push to get out; asset-liability mismatches that were profitable become suddenly unprofitable, making the reversal self-sustaining; capital unavailable so spending stops, growth halts, lenders (especially domestic banks) have debt problems, foreigners lend even less
Printing is limited because it risks enabling more people to get out of the currency; assets go from treasure to trash
Foreign-denominated debt is the key mismatch: debtors sell local currency to repay, hedge and move savings into foreign currency, adding downward pressure
Currency declines push up import prices and inflation; a gradual persistent decline breeds expectations of more decline, capital withdrawal and inflation psychology
Pendulum swings from everything great to everything terrible; debt, economic, political and currency problems reinforce each other; hidden fraud and corruption surface

'Hitting bottom' is the mirror of the bubble (aggressive exit, shortage of buyers); the most severe and painful part, self-reinforcing and rapid; the pain forces a radical change in pricing and policies (catharsis); cheap currency finally cuts imports enough to restore the balance of payments, often with IMF/BIS/multilateral aid and big political shifts

indicators.name: Initial currency depreciation
indicators.typical_reading: On average around 30 percent in real terms (p.49); real FX trough ~-18% vs TWI around month 15 (chart)

indicators.name: Loss from holding the currency
indicators.typical_reading: Not offset by tighter short rates; on average around 30 percent in the first year (p.49); foreign FX return trough ~62 indexed around month 14 (p.50 chart)

indicators.name: Reserves after letting go
indicators.typical_reading: Policy makers keep spending reserves to smooth the fall: on average another 10 percent for a year into the bust (p.49); reserves trough ~82 indexed around month 10 (chart)

indicators.name: Capital inflows
indicators.typical_reading: Dry up, falling fast: by more than 5 percent of GDP in less than 12 months (p.51); ~-3% of GDP trough around months 18-22 (chart)

indicators.name: Capital outflows
indicators.typical_reading: Continue at a pace of -3 to -5 percent of GDP (p.51); trough ~-5% around months 6-8 (chart)

indicators.name: Nominal short rates
indicators.typical_reading: Rise typically by about 20 percentage points and the yield curve inverts (p.52); peak ~35% around months 12-14 (p.48 chart)

indicators.name: Money printing
indicators.typical_reading: Limited: 1 to 2 percent of GDP on average (p.52)

indicators.name: Equities (local currency)
indicators.typical_reading: Fall on average by around 50% in local currency terms, worse in foreign currency terms (p.52); trough ~50 indexed around month 22 from ~120 peak (chart)

indicators.name: Debt service
indicators.typical_reading: Rises further, on average by more than 5 percent of GDP (p.52)

indicators.name: FX debt burden
indicators.typical_reading: Debt-to-GDP rises on average by about 20 percent from the decline in incomes and the currency (p.52); FX debt/GDP ~50% at month 0 to ~72% peak around month 18 (chart)

indicators.name: Total debt (%GDP)
indicators.typical_reading: Peaks ~183% around month 12 from ~160% at month 0 (p.43 chart)

indicators.name: Inflation
indicators.typical_reading: Rises typically by 15 percent, peaking around 30 percent; stays elevated on average about two years from the top (p.53); core inflation ~15% at month 0 to ~35% peak around month 18 (chart)

indicators.name: GDP gap
indicators.typical_reading: Falls a lot, on average by about 8 percent; bottom in activity after about one year with the trough near -4 percent (p.53)

indicators.name: Growth vs potential
indicators.typical_reading: Trough ~-9% around month 14 (p.47 chart)

indicators.name: Unemployment
indicators.typical_reading: Rises (p.53)

indicators.name: Imports
indicators.typical_reading: Contract by around 10 percent through the crisis (p.56); ~+2% to ~-8% indexed trough around months 14-16 (chart)

indicators.name: Exports
indicators.typical_reading: Contract during the worst of the crisis (other countries also slowing), rebound in later years (p.56); trough ~-3.5% around month 18 (chart)

indicators.name: Current account
indicators.typical_reading: From a deficit of -6 percent of GDP to a surplus of 2 percent about 18 months into the crisis (p.56)

policy: Central banks should not defend to the point of letting reserves get too low or rates too high; devaluations are stimulative (assets rise in the weakened currency, exports and margins improve, imports fall, balance of payments adjusts)

Better a large one-off devaluation to a level with a two-way market (no broad expectation of further weakness), ideally a surprise so reserves and rates need not be spent beforehand; hence policy makers say they will defend right up to the moment they stop

Well managed (p.57): bluff then surprise-devalue by enough; tight monetary policy contracts domestic demand in line with the fall in incomes; incentives (rates compensating for depreciation risk) keep investors in the currency; reserves used judiciously to smooth foreign-capital withdrawal; over-indebted entities' debts worked through with credit supplied elsewhere

Poorly managed (p.57): weakness widely expected; initial devaluation too small with more to follow; monetary policy too loose favoring domestic conditions, stoking inflation; capital controls or other restrictions; reserve sales used to sustain spending; disorderly defaults causing uncertainty and capital flight
Recapitalize systemically important institutions and provide targeted liquidity (typically by printing), balanced carefully because it is inflationary (p.55)
inflationary_phases.transition: Supply and demand for the currency rebalance, primarily via capital flows (central bank makes the currency desirable to hold) and secondarily via lower spending and imports; the bottom comes after about one year
inflationary_phases.markets: Currency down ~30% real; equities down ~50% local (worse in foreign currency); short rates up ~20 points with an inverted curve; foreign-currency bond returns collapse (typical cases ~100 to ~68 indexed); gold and foreign assets preferred
inflationary_phases.duration: Bottom in activity after about one year; inflation elevated about two years from the top; months 0 to 36 on the archetype axis

inflationary_phases.name: 5) Normalization
conditions: Balance between supply and demand for the currency relative to other currencies, determined mostly by capital flows: the central bank succeeds in making the currency desirable to hold, and spending/imports have fallen enough to adjust the balance of payments

Policy makers must produce a positive total return for the currency at an acceptable (not too high) interest rate; the currency level that is good for trade, produces a positive total return and allows an appropriate domestic rate is a low one

After a sharp depreciation, total return (spot appreciation plus rate differential) is more likely positive at a low real rate; returns to foreigners start negative then rally about a year after the devaluation

Recovery takes a few years: burned investors are reluctant to return, but cheap domestic goods and labor attract foreign direct investment; protected and recapitalized financial institutions support recovery; the country returns to the early part of the cycle

indicators.name: Current account
indicators.typical_reading: Collapse in imports improves it a lot, on average by about 8 percent of GDP (p.56)

indicators.name: Capital inflows
indicators.typical_reading: Stop declining and stabilize (p.56); return a few years later, on average four to five (p.57)

indicators.name: Capital flight
indicators.typical_reading: Abates (p.56)

indicators.name: IMF/international support
indicators.typical_reading: Frequently sought, especially when reserves are limited (p.56)

indicators.name: Short rates
indicators.typical_reading: Start to come down after about a year while long rates stay elevated; fall back to pre-crisis levels in around two years after peaking (p.56)

indicators.name: Forward currency
indicators.typical_reading: Rallies relative to spot as rates come down (p.56)

indicators.name: Inflation
indicators.typical_reading: Comes down as the currency stabilizes; nearly two years after the bottom to reach pre-crisis levels (p.56)

indicators.name: Incomes and spending
indicators.typical_reading: Pick up usually after about one to two years (p.57)

indicators.name: Activity back to average
indicators.typical_reading: Usually about three years from the bottom (p.57)

indicators.name: Real FX
indicators.typical_reading: Undervalued typically by around 10 percent on a PPP basis at the start of stabilization and stays cheap (p.57)

indicators.name: Exports
indicators.typical_reading: Pick up a bit, by 1 to 2 percent of GDP (p.57)

indicators.name: Equities (foreign currency terms)
indicators.typical_reading: Take about the same time as capital inflows (four to five years) to recover (p.57); local-currency index ~160 by month 84 (chart)

indicators.name: Foreign FX return (indexed)
indicators.typical_reading: ~62 trough to ~100 by month 84 (p.55 chart)

policy: Let the currency depreciate sharply and quickly so that investors expect positive total returns at a relatively low real rate

Central bank objective: a currency cheap enough to stimulate the economy and the balance of payments, with policy tight enough to make owning the currency attractive; devaluation is like cocaine (ruinous when abused); watch what central banks do before going long
Recapitalize systemically important institutions and provide targeted liquidity to manage bad debts, balancing the inflationary effect of printing
inflationary_phases.transition: A new virtuous cycle begins: productive investment opportunities attract capital, capital drives growth and asset prices, attracting more capital
inflationary_phases.markets: Currency stabilizes at a cheap level; foreign holders' returns turn positive about a year after devaluation; short rates fall; equities recover in foreign-currency terms over four to five years
inflationary_phases.duration: Several years: incomes up after 1-2 years, activity to average after about 3, capital inflows and foreign-currency equities after 4-5

inflationary_phases.name: Spiral to hyperinflation (subset of inflationary depressions)
inflationary_phases.months: Depression onward; typical case recovers, subset spirals
conditions: Policy makers don't close the imbalance between external income, external spending and debt service and keep funding external spending for sustained periods by printing lots of money (the most important characteristic)

Weimar's reparations were an external debt that mostly could not be defaulted on, so big inflation was all but destined; elsewhere policy makers choose to keep printing to prop up growth rather than align spending with income

Stopping printing mid-crisis causes extreme illiquidity and deep contraction and gets harder the longer the crisis runs (by late October 1923 Germany's entire 1913 money stock would have bought a one-kilo loaf of rye bread)
Inflationary psychology sets in: currency declines inspire capital flight, an escalating feedback loop of depreciation, inflation and printing; growth linkages weaken
Each round of printing sends more money into real or foreign assets rather than goods and services; stocks stop providing a wealth effect; devaluation stops stimulating growth

Wage-cost spiral (wage demands, price increases, wage indexing); savers short cash and buy foreign and physical assets; depositors and lenders shorten maturities or stop lending (average debt maturities always fall in inflationary deleveragings)

Illiquidity: cheap to short cash as printing lowers real rates; banks cannot meet cash demand; central bank prints again to support banks and lend to businesses, funding more foreign-asset buying and hedging

FX-denominated debt burdens and debt service rise as the currency falls; foreigners demand higher rates for default risk; governments raise income and wealth taxes; the wealthy evade and move capital abroad
Domestic credit creation doesn't produce growth because it is spent on foreign assets and stores of value (gold, factories, imports, even rocks in Weimar)

Money loses its roles as store of value (people hold a few days' reserves), unit of account (too many zeros) and medium of exchange (producers demand foreign currency or barter); illiquidity peaks because foreign exchange is short and cannot be relieved by printing; stores close, unemployment rises, the economy contracts rapidly

Financial wealth wiped out; extreme redistribution (lenders' wealth and debtors' liabilities inflated away); strikes (even police), disorder, crime, looting, violence; Weimar declared a 'state of siege'

indicators.name: Inflation rate
indicators.typical_reading: Prices more than doubling every year or worse (definition, p.58)

indicators.name: Domestic currency bond return (USD, indexed)
indicators.typical_reading: Hyperinflations: ~100 at month 0 to ~10 by month 24 and ~0 from month ~48; typical inflationary depressions: ~100 to ~68 trough around month 12, recovering to ~105 by month 84 (p.59 chart)

indicators.name: Debt maturities
indicators.typical_reading: Always fall during inflationary deleveragings (p.59)

indicators.name: Share prices vs exchange rate
indicators.typical_reading: Increasing divergence as inflation transitions to hyperinflation; shares rise in local currency but are a disaster in real terms; bonds wiped out; gold preferred (p.60)

policy: Investing: get short the currency, get money out of the country, buy commodities and invest in commodity industries (gold, coal, metals); equities a mixed bag and a losing proposition as inflation turns to hyperinflation
Exit: a currency that spirals into hyperinflation never recovers its status as a store hold of wealth; the classic path is creating a new currency with very hard backing while phasing out the old one
inflationary_phases.transition: Ends only with a new hard-backed currency replacing the old one
inflationary_phases.markets: Currency collapse; bonds wiped out; shares rise nominally but lose in real/foreign-currency terms; gold and foreign assets the only stores of value
inflationary_phases.duration: Not quantified; Weimar 1918-1924 is the iconic case (Part 2)

vulnerability_conditions.description: Countries/currencies far more likely to have severe inflationary deleveragings or hyperinflations (p.40)
conditions: Don't have a reserve currency (no global bias to hold the currency/debt as a store hold of wealth)
Have low foreign-exchange reserves (small cushion against capital outflows)
Have a large foreign debt (vulnerable to rising debt costs via interest rates or the currency the debtor must deliver, or a shortage of dollar-denominated credit)
Have a large and increasing budget and/or current account deficit (must borrow or print to fund it)
Have negative real interest rates (lenders inadequately compensated for holding the currency/debt)
Have a history of high inflation and negative total returns in the currency (lack of trust)
notes: The more of these conditions exist, the greater the inflationary depression; the iconic case is Weimar Germany in the early 1920s

Reserve-currency countries without significant foreign-currency debt can have inflationary depressions, but they emerge more slowly and later, after sustained and repeated overuse of stimulation to reverse a deflationary deleveraging; permitting much higher inflation to keep growth strong by printing lots of money undermines demand for the currency and erodes reserve status
About a 75% correlation between the amount of foreign-currency debt and the amount of inflation experienced (p.13)

war_economies.cycle_rule: War risk rises sharply when two conditions coincide: (1) internal conflict between the wealthy/capitalist right and the poor/proletarian left that brings populist, autocratic, nationalistic and militaristic leaders to power, and (2) external rivalry between economic and military powers of comparable strength; economics and politics then become tightly entangled and disruptive conflicts become far more likely than normal (p.61)
relationship_types: Cooperative-competitive (win-win): parties consider what matters to the other and trade for what they most want; tough but respectful negotiation

Mutually threatening (lose-lose): parties try to harm each other to force submission; interaction through 'war' rather than 'negotiation'; either side can force this path, both are needed for the cooperative one
principles: Periods of war are followed by periods of peace in which the dominant power sets the rules until a rival emerges; a 250-year frame is needed to see the rise and fall of empires and reserve currencies

In war the most important economic priority is maintaining access to the financial and non-financial resources required for the war effort; no country can fund a war and tolerable civilian spending from current income, so it needs borrowing capacity (creditworthiness, a sound local-currency debt market) and/or very large FX reserves

After the war, the debts and the outcome (won or lost) have enormous market consequences; the worst thing a country can do is get into a lot of debt and lose a war: 'ABOVE ALL ELSE, DON'T DO THAT' (p.62)

After a major war both winners and losers are saddled with debt and face a postwar recession as military spending contracts; losers experience much deeper depressions, print more money, draw down reserves meaningfully and see much higher inflation, sometimes hyperinflation

deleveraging_levers.effect: Deflationary; reduces debt burdens but cuts incomes as spending is cut; even deep austerity doesn't rebalance debt and income
Deflationary; cleanses bad debts; write-downs must be large enough for debtors to service restructured loans; devastating for leveraged creditors (banks levered ~12:1 to 15:1)

deleveraging_levers.lever: The central bank 'printing money' and making purchases (or providing guarantees) / debt monetization
deleveraging_levers.effect: Inflationary and stimulative; not inflationary when it offsets credit contraction; typically about 4% of GDP per year at the turn

deleveraging_levers.lever: Transfers of money and credit from those who have more than they need to those who have less (wealth redistribution)
deleveraging_levers.effect: Via income, property, consumption taxes; wealth/inheritance taxes raise little; rarely contributes meaningfully to a deleveraging without revolutions

Enough stimulation (printing/monetization and currency devaluation) to offset the deflationary levers (austerity/defaults) and bring nominal growth above the nominal interest rate, so debt/income ratios fall while activity and asset prices improve, without accelerating inflation, a currency devaluation spiral, a run on debt assets or a new debt bubble

monetary_policy_types.name: Monetary Policy 1 (MP1)
monetary_policy_types.description: Interest-rate driven; most effective and broadest impact: positive wealth effect (present values), easier credit purchases (durables, housing), lower debt-service burdens; first approach to a debt crisis; stops working when short rates hit about 0%

monetary_policy_types.name: Monetary Policy 2 (MP2)
monetary_policy_types.description: Quantitative easing: printing money and buying financial assets, typically debt; works via investors/savers who redeploy cash; benefits asset owners and widens the wealth gap; most effective when risk and liquidity premiums are large; loses effectiveness as premiums are compressed; if private credit growth doesn't pick up, policy is pushing on a string; prolonged monetization risks doubts about the currency as a store hold of value

monetary_policy_types.name: Monetary Policy 3 (MP3)
monetary_policy_types.description: Puts money more directly into the hands of spenders and incentivizes them to spend; continuum from coordinated fiscal-monetary action to helicopter money; forms: debt-financed fiscal spending paired with QE; fiscal spending where the Treasury isn't on the hook; printed money given directly to the government (fiat printing or coin debasement); helicopter money to households (equal/targeted, one-off/UBI, use-it-or-lose-it, directed accounts, QE returns to households); big debt write-down with big money creation (year of Jubilee); most effective with fiscal/monetary coordination and spending incentives

monetary_policy_types.name: Macroprudential policies
monetary_policy_types.description: Regulatory powers to influence the cost and availability of credit for targeted parts of the financial system; valuable in all seven stages; explained in the Appendix

bubble_checklist.paraphrase: prices sit high against the usual yardsticks (earnings, rents, incomes)
prices already assume further rapid gains from those high levels
bullishness is broad, not confined to specialists
purchases are financed with a lot of borrowed money
buyers have locked in unusually far ahead - stockpiles, supply contracts, pre-orders - to speculate or to hedge against higher prices
people who were never in the market before are now buying
easy money is still feeding the bubble, and tightening would be what pops it

rules.text: Judge credit growth by what it produces and whether the debt can be serviced; too little credit growth can be as damaging as too much.
The downside of a large debt stock depends on policy makers' willingness and ability to spread the losses, which requires own-currency debt and influence over creditor/debtor behavior.
Debt crises recur because lending is never done perfectly and policy makers err toward easy credit for near-term rewards; it is politically easier to allow easy credit than tight credit.
A classic warning sign of a coming bubble is a rising share of borrowing used to pay debt service; the cycle reverses when debt-service costs exceed what can be borrowed.
In a crisis, deal with the lending institutions first; the most leveraged lenders with the most concentrated exposures pose the biggest knock-on risks.
Almost every own-currency debt crisis can be managed well; the biggest risks are policy makers' lack of knowledge and authority and the politics of who bears the pain, not the debts themselves.
The key to handling a crisis: know how to use the levers, have the authority to use them, and know the rate per year at which burdens are spread and who benefits and suffers.
Four levers (austerity, defaults/restructurings, printing/monetization, wealth transfers) must be balanced to produce a beautiful deleveraging.
Central banks should target debt growth at a sustainable level (income growth sufficient to service it) rather than only inflation and growth; ignoring bubbles is imprudent.
No single aggregate metric indicates an impending crisis; examine individual entities' debt-service capacity and the concentration of debt.
Tops are made when things are so good they can't get better yet everyone believes they will.
The size of the downturn depends on each sector's sensitivity to tightening and how losses cascade, not mainly on the size of the tightening; analyze sectors and big players, not averages.
Immediately after a bubble bursts the wealth effect dominates monetary policy; do not mistake the early decline for a buying opportunity because earnings have not yet fallen.
Solvency problems need equity capital or rule changes; cash-flow problems need cash or guarantees; both can be provided by fiscal/monetary policy when the debt is in the home currency.
Depressions are driven by the supply and demand for credit, money, goods and services, not primarily by psychology.
Policy makers initially get the mix wrong and act slowly out of taxpayer anger and moral-hazard fears; the longer stimulus is delayed, the uglier the deleveraging.
Austerity and tax increases in a depression are big mistakes.
When systemically important institutions risk failing, act immediately: curtail panic and guarantee liabilities, provide liquidity, support solvency, and recapitalize/nationalize/cover losses.

Best-managed cases swiftly recognize the magnitude, don't save every expendable institution, restore credit pipes and keep growth and inflation acceptable during the workout; speed and aggressiveness determine severity and length.
Protect small depositors; let equity, subordinated debt and large depositors absorb losses; keep paying IMF/BIS loans to preserve lender-of-last-resort access.
Rich and poor sharing a budget in a downturn produces economic and political conflict and populism; how well this is handled determines how the society weathers the period.
For debt burdens to fall, nominal income growth must exceed nominal interest rates; printing that merely offsets credit contraction is not inflationary.
Avoid printing too much money; getting the balance right is harder with foreign-currency debt held by foreigners.
In the end policy makers always print; doing it quickly and well produces much better results than doing it late.

The right amount of stimulus neutralizes the deflationary credit collapse and gets nominal growth above nominal rates by enough to relieve debt burdens, but not so much that it causes a run on debt assets.

Use MP1 (rates) first; MP2 (QE) works while risk premiums are high and fades as they compress; MP3 (money to spenders) when both are exhausted; fiscal-monetary coordination with incentives to spend is most effective.
Expect roughly 5 to 10 years for activity and about a decade for equities to regain prior peaks after a deflationary deleveraging.
If a currency is expected to fall faster than its interest rate compensates, holders exit; when money flows out, real rates must rise less if the real exchange rate falls more, and vice versa.
Currency weakness is what makes a depression inflationary; the squeeze ends through defaults or money creation, debt-service relief, or depreciation that exceeds the rise in inflation.

Vulnerability screen: no reserve currency, low FX reserves, large foreign debt, large and rising budget/current-account deficits, negative real rates, a history of high inflation and negative currency returns.
Capital flows are the most important flows to watch because they are the most volatile.
Reserve sales, rate hikes and managed declines typically fail to defend a currency; capital controls seldom work and are at best a temporary fix.
Do not defend the currency to the point of dangerously low reserves or dangerously high rates; devaluations are stimulative.
Prefer a large, surprise, one-off devaluation that creates a two-way market over a gradual decline; say you will defend right up to the moment you stop.
The currency level that is good for the trade balance, produces a positive total return and allows an appropriate domestic interest rate is a low one; depreciate sharply and quickly.
Devaluing currencies is like using cocaine: short-term stimulus, ruinous when abused; watch what the central bank does before going long the currency.
The central bank's objective after devaluation: a currency cheap enough to stimulate the economy and balance of payments, with policy tight enough to make owning the currency attractive.
Hyperinflation follows when policy makers keep funding external imbalances by printing for sustained periods; stopping printing mid-crisis is extremely hard and gets harder with time.

In a hyperinflation: short the currency, move money out of the country, hold commodities and commodity industries (gold preferred); shares and bonds are losers; the exit is a new hard-backed currency.
In war, maintain access to financial and non-financial resources via borrowing capacity and reserves; above all, never run up big debts and lose a war.
Managing debt crises is about spreading out the pain of bad debts; the main risk is policy failure from lack of knowledge or authority; foreign-currency debt makes everything harder and more painful.
In the long run productivity matters far more than debt crises, but their political consequences (populism) can be more consequential than the crises themselves.
